name: Sara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married into Hillcrest, my husband Adam's family farm, sixteen years ago. We keep about 250 dairy goats, grow hay and oats, and I make cheese with my mother-in-law Halima in the old stone dairy. My mornings are milking, then the cheese room, then labels, orders and the market stall on Saturdays. Adam does the fields and the machinery with his father Ismail. We live in our own house at the top of the lane, which is where the mortgage comes in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Doing three jobs at once, mother, farmer, cheesemaker. Hana's thirteen and Bilal's ten, and they both help at kidding time, which I love. I'll use an AI tool now and then to write a cheese description or a post for the stall, but Halima doesn't trust it. She says if a machine can describe the cheese, it should try making it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine with me. It's what I'd expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy little helper for the paperwork and that's all. Good cheese still needs good hands, and no computer is going to change that. I'd say that at the stall if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. Our cheese sells because it's made by a family, by hand, and that wouldn't change. The worries stay the same, feed costs, the vet bill and whether the Saturday market keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are. I'd use the AI a bit more for the stall's posts and maybe the bookkeeping. We'd keep putting 150 a month aside and maybe buy a second cheese vat next year, about 4,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Halima make of the AI writing your cheese descriptions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She read one out loud at dinner in a funny posh voice and the kids laughed for ten minutes. Then she said, fine, but it forgot to mention the thyme. She was right, it did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here you'd want to change on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe a better milking system for the goats, once a few other goat farms have one. We're not the kind to be first.

S0.say: It's a handy little helper for the paperwork and that's all. Good cheese still needs good hands, and no computer is going to change that.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because our cheese sells for being made by hand by a family. The worries stay feed costs, the vet bill and whether the Saturday market keeps going.
S0.do: Keeps going as the family always has and uses AI a little more for posts and bookkeeping. Keeps saving 150 a month and considers a second cheese vat for about 4,000.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: Then she said, fine, but it forgot to mention the thyme.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's identity is bound up with handmade family cheese. She uses AI lightly and only for words, never the craft. Her mother-in-law's scepticism is affectionate and shapes the household's attitude.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's closer to what Adam reads about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families who work hard and look after each other will be fine. You change what you need to and keep what matters. I'd say that to friends at the mosque and to the other stallholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit about cheap cheese. If big dairies get robots that make decent goat cheese for half our cost, the people who just want a cheap cheese stop coming to the stall. We'd keep the customers who care, but there might be fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see how the robot milking systems do on two or three goat farms before we touch one. We'd save a bit more, 200 a month, and hold off on the second vat. I'd try selling to two restaurants in town, so we're not just relying on the stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small worry that sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Adam and Ismail say about robot milking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Adam would want it tomorrow, he loves machines. Ismail would say his father milked by hand and so did he. I'd be in the middle, as usual, and probably the one who decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help farms like yours, if things got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the community. I don't want the government paying us to make cheese. If we can't sell it, we should make something people will buy.

S1.say: Families who work hard and look after each other will be fine. You change what you need to and keep what matters.
S1.think: I'd worry about cheap cheese: if big dairies get robots that make decent goat cheese for half our cost, the bargain hunters stop coming to the stall. We'd keep the customers who care, but fewer of them.
S1.do: Waits to see robot milking working on two or three goat farms before considering one. Raises savings to 200 a month, holds off the second vat and tries selling to two restaurants in town.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a small worry that stays put.
S1.quote: I don't want the government paying us to make cheese. If we can't sell it, we should make something people will buy.
S1.fieldNote: Sara sits between her husband's love of machines and her father-in-law's tradition, and is likely the decider. She looks for new customers rather than outside help. Her worry is cheaper competition, not losing her own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before Hana's even finished school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we trust in God and look after our own. I'd say it at the mosque and to the family, and I'd mean it. I wouldn't post anything about it, people online just argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. If everyone's work goes at once, who buys handmade cheese at a market stall? Our customers are teachers, office people, nurses. If they lose their wages, we lose our customers in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop every extra right away, no new vat, no holiday to Adam's cousins. We'd move savings into paying down the mortgage. I'd sell more cheese wholesale, even at a lower price, to keep money coming in, and we'd lean on Ismail and Halima, who own the farm outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the night a goat gets stuck kidding and you don't know if you'll save her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the stall in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it going as long as people came. Even if I sold half as much, it's where people know us. You don't give up your place at the market, it took Halima twenty years to get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about robots on the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years? We couldn't afford them and we wouldn't know which ones work. I'd rather keep milking by hand and keep our costs low. That's the only thing I'd be sure of.

S2.say: We trust in God and look after our own. I'd say it at the mosque and to the family, but I wouldn't post anything because people online just argue.
S2.think: If everyone's work goes at once, who buys handmade cheese at a market stall? Our customers are teachers, office people and nurses, and if they lose their wages we lose them in the same year.
S2.do: Stops every extra, including the vat and the family holiday, and moves savings into paying down the mortgage. Sells more cheese wholesale at a lower price and leans on her in-laws, who own the farm outright.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a difficult kidding when she doesn't know if she'll save the goat.
S2.quote: You don't give up your place at the market, it took Halima twenty years to get it.
S2.fieldNote: Sara's fear in fast AGI is about customers, not machines. She turns to faith and family, and her in-laws' ownership of the land is her safety net. She'd refuse robots she can't afford or trust in a two-year rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit easier to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to get ready together, and young people should learn trades that still matter. I'd say that at the mosque youth group, where I help on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd survive, but smaller. Handmade cheese might become a luxury, sold to fewer people for more. If a few other goat farms prove the robot milkers by year two or three, we'd probably get one so I have more time for the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving 200 a month and start selling cheese online with the AI's help, to reach people outside our town. I'd watch the robot milkers on other goat farms and, if they work, put about 10,000 into one in year three. And I'd make sure Hana takes her exams seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as frightened as with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you'd refuse robots. Why consider one now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by year three I'd have seen them work on farms like ours. I'm not against machines, I'm against being the first fool to buy one. Five years gives other people time to make the mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she should learn something useful with her hands and her head, and stay close to family. She'd be eighteen by 2031. If she wants to make cheese with me, she's welcome, but I'd want her to have another skill too.

S3.say: Families and communities need to get ready together, and young people should learn trades that still matter. I'd say that at the mosque youth group where I help on Fridays.
S3.think: We'd survive, but smaller, with handmade cheese becoming a luxury sold to fewer people for more. If other goat farms prove the robot milkers by year two or three, we'd probably get one so I have more time for the cheese.
S3.do: Keeps saving 200 a month and starts selling cheese online with AI's help. Puts about 10,000 into a robot milker in year three if it's proven on other goat farms, and makes sure Hana takes her exams seriously.
S3.feel: Anxious, but less frightened than with two years.
S3.quote: I'm not against machines, I'm against being the first fool to buy one.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Sara's steady approach work: watch others, then buy. She'd shift her cheese towards a smaller luxury market and online sales. She wants her daughter to have a second skill beyond the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Bilal would be twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so people should stop worrying and start preparing. Look after your family, learn what you need to learn. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not too worried about this one. We'd have time to try robots once they're proven, keep the cheese side going and see how the customers change. The thing I'd think about most is what work there'd be for Hana and Bilal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait two or three years and watch, then buy a robot milker once it's cheap and proven, maybe 8,000 by then. I'd build up the online cheese sales slowly. We'd start a small fund for the children's training, 50 a month each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but calm enough. Ten years feels like time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ismail and Halima still be on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ismail would be in his late seventies, Halima too. I think they'd still be in the dairy, telling us we're doing it wrong. I'd want them to see the robots work before they stop, so they know the farm will go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss if robots did the milking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet half hour at six with the goats. That's my time to think. I'd probably still go down and sit with them anyway.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, so people should stop worrying and start preparing. Look after your family and learn what you need to learn.
S4.think: I'm not too worried about this one: there's time to try proven robots, keep the cheese going and watch how customers change. What I'd think about most is what work there'd be for Hana and Bilal.
S4.do: Watches for two or three years, then buys a proven robot milker for about 8,000. Builds online cheese sales slowly and starts funds of 50 a month for each child's training.
S4.feel: Uneasy but calm enough, with time to breathe.
S4.quote: The quiet half hour at six with the goats. That's my time to think.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits Sara's wait-for-proof style, and she'd adopt robots once cheap. Her attention shifts to her children's futures and to her ageing in-laws seeing the farm continue. She'd miss quiet time with the goats.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our customers would lose their wages before we'd had time to find new ones. What would help is time and family, and maybe help to sell our cheese further away, but not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats themselves. People think farming is about money, but some mornings it's just about a kid that wasn't breathing and now is. A robot doesn't feel that.

headlineQuote: Some mornings it's just about a kid that wasn't breathing and now is.
portrait: Sara Ibrahim, 43, married into Hillcrest, her husband's family goat farm, where she makes handmade cheese with her mother-in-law and runs a Saturday market stall. She uses AI now and then for labels and posts, trusts family and faith over government and waits for others to prove new machines. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy about cheap robot cheese under steady change. Fast AGI alarms her because her customers would lose their wages; with more time she'd adopt proven robot milkers and sell cheese online.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her customers would lose their wages before she could find new ones.
whatWouldHelp: Time, family, and help selling cheese further afield, but not handouts.
